article.heading: Online streamer
article.intro: An online streamer or live streamer is a type of social media influencer who broadcasts themselves online through a live stream to an audience.

sections.heading: History
sections.text: Online streaming arose in the mid-to-late 2000s, originating on sites like YouTube where users could upload videos of themselves in the form of vlogs or Let's Plays. While not all content featured a live audience, users were still able to gain a sizable following and make a living from their content. Other sites like Twitch increased this popularity by offering innovations such as video clippings and pay-for-play. Due to the potential for high earnings from multiple income streams, including ad revenue sharing, endorsements, partnerships, and subscriptions, streaming has become a much-yearned-for career option.

subsections.heading: Video games
subsections.text: Let's Plays have been the most popular streamers by far since the beginning of live streaming. Today, the majority of streamers make their living from doing Let's Plays, live speedruns, and walkthroughs of video games. The biggest video game streamers are PewDiePie and Ninja, who make millions of dollars each year just from streaming.

subsections.heading: IRL streams
subsections.text: While the majority of professional and part-time streamers play video games, many often do IRL (in real life) streams where they broadcast their daily life. Topics include answering questions in front of a computer, streaming from their phone while walking outside, or doing tutorials.

subsections.heading: Virtual avatar
subsections.text: Virtual avatars, commonly known as VTubers, are a branch of streaming in which virtual avatars, occasionally paired with voice changers, are used instead of the streamer's face. Companies focused on the promotion, support, and merchandising of VTuber talent include Nijisanji and Hololive Production. In 2020, there were more than 10,000 active VTubers.

subsections.heading: Pornographic streaming
subsections.text: Pornographic streams are a way to directly communicate with porn stars. Camgirls and camboys broadcast while nude or performing sexual acts often on demand from viewers. Sites like Plexstorm have created a niche by streaming video gamers performing or showing sexual content including pornographic games.

subsections.heading: Trash streaming
subsections.text: A controversial form of live broadcasting where the host engages in shocking, dangerous, or humiliating activities, often to drive viewer donations. Popular primarily in Russia, Ukraine, and Poland, this format has also been observed in Finland and is associated with sensationalist content meant to provoke or entertain through extreme behavior.

subsections.heading: Marathon/lifestream streaming
subsections.text: Some streamers broadcast nearly all aspects of daily life for prolonged periods. For example, a Twitch streamer known only as Emily streamed continuously for over 1,100 days, sharing routines, meals, and personal moments, highlighting the emotional toll and blurred boundaries of online performance culture.

subsections.heading: South Korea
subsections.text: In South Korea, a streamer is called a broadcast jockey. Broadcast jockeys have become popular over the years in Korea thanks in part to many of them being more relatable to viewers than some celebrities and becoming famous enough to appear on TV shows. Korean sites include AfreecaTV, Naver TV, and KakaoTV in addition to worldwide streaming sites like Twitch, YouTube, and Bigo Live. Mukbang, the live-streaming of eating a meal, originated in South Korea.

subsections.heading: China
subsections.text: China has become the largest marketplace for live streaming. A large number of streamers make $10,000-$100,000 a month without having to be a big name on the Internet. This is due to the large population and the ubiquity of smartphones. Chinese streaming sites may be restricted to Chinese content and audiences due to strict Internet rules in the country.
